1222-cobb-s-anatomy:
Irvin S. Cobb, a Kentucky humorist famed for his newspaper columns, turns his comic eye on the human body in this book. Chapters on tummies, teeth, hair, hands, and feet mix tall tales, doctor jokes, and mock science, all in Cobb's easy, drawling voice.

The humor is homely and old-style: fat men and their vests, dentists and their drills, and the trials of getting old. Cobb never aims high, but his jokes land with warmth. The book suits readers who like gentle American humor and a laugh at the body's frailties.
12417-fishin-jimmy:
Annie Trumbull Slosson's 1889 story opens at Franconia, a peaceful village among New Hampshire hills, on the margin of Pond Brook behind Uncle Eben's. Boys tempt trout with fly or worm while the narrator roams for spring flowers and butterflies, until a voice cries Strike him, sonny, and an old man steps noiselessly through the bushes.

That man is Fishin' Jimmy, spare, wiry, stooped, with a thin brown face, a local angler and storyteller. Slosson lets Jimmy's talk, humour and country wisdom carry a gentle tale of village life and nature. The book is a small, warm sketch, valued for its dialect voice and its affection for New Hampshire streams and summers.
13020-the-boy-allies-at-verdun-or-saving:
Clair W. Hayes set The Boy Allies at Verdun in February 1916, on the eve of the war's most bitter battle to that date. An automobile speeds north along a French line held for nearly two years, carrying a youth of eighteen in a British lieutenant's uniform and two companions. German armies press toward the heart of France.

A night infiltration scene finds Hal and Chester watching German troopers dig breastworks, wandering among them, then sprinting for trees at Hal's whispered word. Hayes keeps the action close and fast. Young readers got here a vivid Verdun tale from the war's own years.
15636-the-future-of-astronomy:
Edward C. Pickering, of Harvard College Observatory, wrote this essay on the future of star study, reprinted from Popular Science Monthly of August 1909. Pickering claims star study is not only the oldest science but the most advanced, since no other science has had such backing from kings, the state, and rich givers. Recent years, he notes, gave star watchers larger jobs than any other branch of pure science.

Physics, Pickering admits, pays better in use: the phone, power sent by wire, wireless, and the sea cable all grew from deep rules, with huge cash gains. Yet few labs for pure study exist, except those paid for by the state. Star study, by contrast, commands fine scopes, tools, and gifts. Pickering looks ahead to bigger scopes, sky maps, and lists, and to a science growing by big, planned work.
15644-thirteen-months-in-the-rebel-army:
William G. Stevenson, an impressed New Yorker, published this Civil War narrative in New York in 1862, with A. S. Barnes and Burr. The subtitle promises personal adventures in the infantry, ordnance, cavalry, courier, and hospital services, with an exhibition of the power, purposes, earnestness, military despotism, and demoralization of the South. A frontispiece shows a council of war before Pittsburg Landing.

Chapter one tells how Stevenson volunteered, went to Arkansas, faced questions on slavery, and met Judge Lynch at midnight. Butler Cavins and his lariat, an acquittal, and an attempted escape follow. Later chapters trace his service across the rebel army's branches, ending in hospital work. The book is a rare insider account: a Northern man trapped in Southern uniform, watching the Confederacy from inside its ranks.
15962-essays-on-political-economy:
A set of essays on political economy by Frederic Bastiat, member of the Institute of France, in the third People's Edition. G. P. Putnam's Sons issued it in New York in 1874, with a London printing by Provost and Company. Bastiat, a French liberal, argues for free trade and limited government in plain, witty prose. His essays made him famous across Europe.

Capital and Interest opens with a sack of corn, a house, and a plane, showing how capital earns its return. That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen, follows, with the broken window, disbanding troops, taxes, theatres, and public works. Machinery, credit, Algeria, and frugality and luxury close the lesson. Bastiat's book still teaches economics by parable: look past the seen gain to the unseen cost.
16078-the-amateur-army:
Patrick MacGill's 1915 memoir tells how a working man joined Kitchener's Army and learned to be a soldier. Chapters run from enlisting and billeting through rations and sick parade, pickets and special leave, officers and rifles, the coffee shop, and the night side of soldiering. Divisional exercise, mimic warfare, a general's inspection, and endless waiting lead at last to the battalion moving off.

MacGill, author of Children of the Dead End, writes in a plain, wry voice about army routine, boredom, and comradeship. His book is not a battle history but a recruit's-eye view of training in wartime Britain. Readers of First World War memoirs will find it honest, funny, and human.
16227-the-uses-of-astronomy:
Edward Everett delivered this oration at Albany on August 28, 1856, for the inauguration of the Dudley Astronomical Observatory. Published in New York by Ross and Tousey, the volume adds a condensed report of the proceedings and an account of dedicating New York State Geological Hall. Everett argues the uses of astronomy for science, navigation, farming, and the wider life of a republic.

The explanatory note hopes the record will spread as fast as the newspaper editions sold out, for the good of science. Everett's eloquence, famous in his day, turns telescopes and stars into civic pride. Readers of American science history will find a stately, hopeful document from the age of observatory building.
16750-the-colored-regulars-in-the-united:
Chaplain T. G. Steward of the Twenty-fifth U.S. Infantry wrote this 1904 history of Black regulars in the United States Army, issued by the A. M. E. Book Concern in Philadelphia. A letter from Lieutenant-General Nelson A. Miles opens the book. It sketches Black American history and Black service in war from the Revolution through 1899, with chapters on the Revolution, 1812, the Civil War, and the Black regulars.

Steward writes to record service long slighted, with care for units, battles, and social roots. His tone is proud and factual, aimed at readers who want the full army story. The book remains a key early history of Black soldiers, valued for its scope and for its first-hand military voice.
18579-taken-by-the-enemy:
Oliver Optic published this boys' naval novel at Boston in 1888, first in his Blue and Gray Afloat series. It follows Captain Horatio Passford and his son Christy aboard the steam yacht Bellevite, with news from shore, a brother in the South, and a mission toward Mobile Bay. Chapters trace the Bellevite past Fort Morgan, a prisoner taken, a rebellion in the pilot house, and a cannon ball through the Leopard.

Christy matures a scheme, finds himself a prisoner, and helps run the gantlet in the closing chapters. Optic keeps the action brisk and the seamanship plain. The book is a rousing Civil War sea tale for young readers.
18800-last-enemy:
H. Beam Piper's story, from Astounding Science Fiction of August 1950, opens at a feast where Dallona of Hadron fidgets over an experiment not yet complete. Beside her sits Garnon of Roxor, who decided long before to take a step that gives her work its test, waiting only until after the election.

At the table sit Girzon, the armed Dirzed with his scarlet winged patch, and a bearded man praising a boy sensitive now in a trance at a writing machine. The boy, a low-grade imbecile awake, once produced a message from the discarnate Assassin Sirzim. The story's blurb names its theme: a pattern of belief that makes assassination an honorable profession, and a last enemy tougher than all the rest.
1905-the-governess-or-the-little-female-:
Sarah Fielding's Governess, or The Little Female Academy, published in 1749, is one of the first novels written for girls. It opens in the north of England, where a gentlewoman undertakes the education of young ladies and discharges the trust faithfully, instructing those committed to her care in lessons and in manners.

The girls tell stories, quarrel, and learn, and the book's design is moral without being dull: each tale teaches a fault and its cure. Fielding, sister of Henry Fielding, writes with clarity and kindness. The book remains a landmark in children's literature, showing the school story taking shape a century before it became a genre.
19471-badge-of-infamy:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction novel of Mars, first issued in paperback in the early nineteen seventies. Feldman, an amateur pilot, crash-lands with Chris and must learn to live on a world where Earth settlers are turning, body and mind, into Martians. A strange growth spreads along nerves toward the brain.

The plot mixes survival, medicine, and politics: what the change means, who fears it, and whether becoming Martian is a disease or a new birth. Del Rey uses the puzzle to ask how far humans should go to belong on another world, and what price identity pays.
21417-forty-six-years-in-the-army:
John M. Schofield, a lieutenant-general of the United States Army, tells his own career in Forty-Six Years in the Army. The book came out in 1897 and opens with his birth at Gerry, New York, in 1831. His father was a Baptist pastor and later a home missionary in the West.

Schofield traces his path from West Point, where he knew General Winfield Scott, through long service. The contents promise chapters on training, command, and the great wars of his time. He offers the book to young citizens whose skill must guard the Union. It is a senior soldier's plain record of a full life.
22095-the-red-cross-girls-with-the-russi:
Margaret Vandercook sent her Red Cross Girls to a new front in The Red Cross Girls with the Russian Army, published in 1916. Her heroines were American girls doing war relief in Europe. In this volume, Eugenia and her friends reach the eastern war. Eugenia risks her liberty, and nearly her life, by hiding a Belgian officer and his family.

With her help the officer wins papers from the enemy and escapes back to King Albert's army. Russian hospitals, refugees, and spies fill the rest of the tale. Vandercook wrote for girl readers who followed the war in the newspapers. The series gave them heroines their own age inside the great events of 1914 to 1918.
22135-the-moral-economy:
Ralph Barton Perry, a young Harvard philosopher, published The Moral Economy in 1909. Perry opens with Bishop Butler's words on provident living. Morality, he argues with Butler, is neither mystery nor mere custom. It is the observance of the laws by which a life is well and wisely spent, like a household run with care.

Perry treats morals as an economy of interests, values, and choices. He asks how competing goods can be ordered without waste of life. The style is clear and argumentative, aimed at students. Perry later won fame as William James's biographer and editor. This early book shows the practical, Jamesian cast of his thought about value and action.
23744-ahead-of-the-army:
W. O. Stoddard published Ahead of the Army in 1903, a boys' novel of the Mexican-American War. Its chapters move from far-away guns and the race of the Goshawk through the fortune of war and a norther storm. They reach the land of the Montezumas, General Scott and his army, and the Stars and Stripes in Tenochtitlan.

Ned, the young hero, carries despatches, stands under fire, and sees a lance pointed at his bosom. Señor Carfora is trapped, mountain passes are crossed, and a revolution brews. Stoddard, who also wrote The Errand Boy of Andrew Jackson, gives young readers a march to Mexico City with drums, dust, and danger in good measure.
238-dear-enemy:
Sallie McBride, Judy's college friend, inherits a job she never wanted: running the John Grier orphan asylum. Jean Webster's Dear Enemy, told in letters, opens at Christmas when Judy and Jervis hand Sallie the home's reform. A Scotch doctor arrives as bait, and Sallie sees through the trick.

Her letters mix complaints, budgets, and growing affection for children and doctor alike. Sallie reforms diet, discipline, and daily life with humor and grit. The sequel to Daddy-Long-Legs stands on its own as a comedy of work. Webster's letters keep the story brisk and warm.
24440-surgical-anatomy:
Joseph Maclise, fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, wrote this surgical anatomy, with sixty-eight coloured plates, published by Blanchard and Lea in Philadelphia in 1859. Maclise inscribes the work to the gentlemen with whom, as a fellow-student, he was associated at London University College. He records a debt of gratitude to Samuel Cooper and Robert Liston, distinguished professors of that institution. From them he and his fellows inherited an aspiration for the light of science.

The preface states the work's object: to present to medical students, and to practitioners far from the schools, a series of dissections. These dissections show how the chief regions of the human body lie in relation to one another. The transcriber notes that the original book's binding had disintegrated after some 140 years, while its paper, printing, and multicolor images survived in amazingly good condition. Readers get surgical anatomy, plate by plate.
24770-a-prisoner-of-morro-or-in-the-hand:
Issued in 1898 under the name Ensign Clark Fitch, a pen name used by Upton Sinclair, this boys' adventure is set in the Spanish-American War. Young naval cadet Clif Faraday chases a prize, fights boarders, and ends up a prisoner in Morro Castle at Havana, with its dungeon vaults below. Plots by the villain Ignacio and the courage of friends shape his fate.

The story moves fast from sea chases to escapes, recapture, and a bold game of bluff, closing with an appeal on behalf of humanity and the Maine's sailors. Sinclair, writing young, gives readers action, honor, and a clear view of war at sea. It remains a lively period piece from the year of the Maine.
24986-tommy:
Joseph Hocking's 1916 book, published by Hodder and Stoughton, tells the story of 'Tommy,' the British private, from the testimony of the men themselves. Hocking met Tommy before he joined the army, addressing recruiting meetings for more than six months, then followed him through training camps and to France and Flanders. He stood with him near La Bassée and Neuve Chapelle, and at Ypres in trenches within a hundred yards of German sandbags, under shell fire and machine guns.

Only a small part of the story is imagination: nearly every incident was told to Hocking by Tommy himself, though the setting is fiction. Training camp brought hard work, strict discipline, and many duties, yet good fellowship made the lads healthier in body and morals than they had been at home. The book is a tribute from a civilian who tried hard to know his subject.
26014-practical-taxidermy:
Montagu Browne, curator of the town museum at Leicester, teaches amateurs to collect, preserve, and set up natural history specimens in Practical Taxidermy, second edition, revised and enlarged. A chapter on the pictorial arrangement of museums closes the book. Browne says hundreds of letters from readers of the first edition urged the revision, with new methods in modeling and artistic taxidermy.

Directions run practical: skin a fish as told, stuff head with peat and face and fins with putty, lay the skin cut upward, and ladle dry plaster from the tail end. Sew up with care, shorten the skin to make it deep not long, and ram plaster well with a short stick. A plate shows a peregrine falcon in flight and its binding. The manual is a hands on guide to lifelike mounts.
26556-myths-and-marvels-of-astronomy:
Richard A. Proctor gathered these essays into a new edition with Longmans, Green and Company in 1896, after a career writing popular astronomy. His preface says the chief charm of astronomy for many readers lies not in wonders alone, but in lore, legends, and strange fancies from old times. He promises to avoid technical terms where he can, writing for readers outside his own branch of study.

Twelve essays follow, from astrology and the religion of the Great Pyramid to Swedenborg's visions of other worlds and suns in flames. The rings of Saturn, comets as portents, the lunar hoax, and the origin of constellation figures each get a chapter. Old myths and new marvels share the book, with paradoxes and fancies weighed against what recent astronomy had revealed.
2868-the-green-mummy:
Fergus Hume wrote The Green Mummy as a mystery that starts with lovers and a professor, then deepens into a tomb, an inquest, and a string of manuscripts. Professor Braddock's orderly life mixes scientific reading after dinner with work renewed at seven each evening. A mummy, a baronet, a sea captain, and a Spanish don and his daughter upset it. Chapters promise the unexpected twice over, and Hume keeps the promise.

Clues pile up through accusations, circumstantial evidence, confessions, and a letter that reopens the past. The mummy itself links an Egyptian tomb to an English village crime. The novel rewards readers who enjoy an old-fashioned puzzle with romance, a patient detective trail, and a solution that ties the tomb to the living.
29691-taxidermy:
Leon L. Pray wrote this short handbook for the sportsman amateur, printed in New York in MCMXVI as number 47 of the Outing Handbooks. He sets out plain, workable ways to preserve trophies taken afield with gun or rod, aimed at the beginner who loves fine detail and has a fair share of patience. The book does not try to match the long works written for men who make taxidermy their trade.

Six chapters cover tools and stuff, a bird, a small mammal, game fish and small reptiles, a Virginia deer head, and a coyote. Each gives the steps in order, from skinning and cleaning to setting up and finishing the mount. Pray's tone is that of a skilled friend at the bench, and the book still serves as a clear first guide to the craft.
30295-the-social-work-of-the-salvation-a:
Edwin Gifford Lamb, A.B., studies The Social Work of the Salvation Army. A Columbia University dissertation from New York in 1909, submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in political science, carries it. Lamb uses social in his title to signal that, save in an auxiliary way, he does not attempt to describe the religious features of the organization. That field is kept separate for clearness and impartial study.

Commander Booth-Tucker, leader of the Army in the United States from 1896 to 1904, gives the primary division in Lamb's terms. The Army evolved from two great ideas: reaching with the gospel of salvation the masses outside ordinary church influence, and caring for their temporal as well as spiritual interests. With little authentic literature on the subject, Lamb draws primarily on personal observation, visiting Salvation Army social institutions of every description.
31333-the-disfranchisement-of-the-negro-:
John L. Love's 1899 paper for the American Negro Academy examines the legal assault on Black political rights in the American South. Love opens with a line from Edmund Burke, quoted in the text. He argues that the attack works through the forms of law rather than open force. Its aim is political subjection followed by social degradation. He denies that it answers any temporary emergency or a mere question of numbers.

Love traces the roots of this animus into the past and presents the campaign as a deliberate, desperate effort of what he calls the spirit of tyranny. The paper is a compact piece of turn-of-the-century Black political thought. It helps readers see disfranchisement not as a single law but as a system built to strip the vote and its protections.
33219-political-economy:
W. Stanley Jevons's Political Economy, in the Science Primers series and published in New York in 1880, offers a short, clear introduction to economics for general readers. Jevons, professor of political economy at University College, London, states in his preface that he tried to put the truths of political economy into plain form. His chapters run from introduction and utility, through production of wealth, division of labor, and capital, to distribution, wages, trades-unions, and cooperation.

Later chapters treat tenure of land, exchange, money, credit and banking, credit cycles, the functions of government, and taxation, giving a complete primer in sixteen short steps. Jevons writes with the precision of a logician and the clarity of a teacher. The book remains a classic introduction to classical economics, and a good first step for readers who want the foundations of the subject without a heavy textbook.
3474-jeremy:
Hugh Walpole writes a novel of boyhood about Jeremy Cole. Jeremy wakes on the morning of December 8, 1892, aware that he is eight years old for the first time in his life. The chapters follow his birthday, the family dog, a Christmas pantomime, a sea captain, family pride, religion, and a visit to a cow farm. A merry go round and a long wait for Hamlet also figure.

Walpole tells the story close to Jeremy's own view, where small events carry great weight and grown ups remain half understood. The boy is obedient and his word can be trusted, yet he tests the rules of home and school. The novel suits readers who enjoy careful, warm stories of childhood in late Victorian England.
34834-a-text-book-of-astronomy:
A Text-Book of Astronomy was written by George Comstock, director of the Washburn Observatory and professor of astronomy at the University of Wisconsin. Appleton and Company published it in New York in 1903, in the Twentieth Century Text-Books series. A frontispiece shows a total solar eclipse, from photographs of the eclipse of May 1900.

The book teaches in order. It begins with kinds of measurement, of angles and of time, then the stars and their daily motion. Fixed and wandering stars follow, and how to find the planets. A chapter on celestial mechanics sets out Kepler's laws, Newton's laws of motion, gravitation, perturbations, and the discovery of Neptune. The earth as a planet, eclipses, and the instruments of the observatory, telescope, camera and spectroscope, carry the student onward. Comstock wrote for college classes at the opening of the modern observatory age.
35540-the-great-white-army:
Max Pemberton's novel The Great White Army retells Napoleon's invasion of Russia and the retreat from Moscow; Cassell published it in 1916. Pemberton's note gives the scale of the disaster. In his figures, 600,000 men crossed the River Niemen in June 1812. Only 20,000 famished, frost-bitten spectres came back over the Bridge of Kovno in December.

The narrator is Surgeon-Major Constant, who fled Paris in the Revolution of 1792. He studied medicine at Leipsic and followed the Grand Army to Moscow. His story mixes his own march with the exploits of his nephew, Captain Leon de Courcelles of the Velites of the Guard. Their chapters end at the crossing of the Beresina and the last review.
36541-unto-this-last-and-other-essays-on:
John Ruskin's essays on political economy were gathered in a London edition of 1912. Its first part is The Political Economy of Art, lectures read at Manchester, on the discovery, application, accumulation, and distribution of art. Notes added later treat trial schools, the right to public support, and the economy of literature.

The second part is Unto This Last, in four essays: the roots of honour, the veins of wealth, a Latin-titled third, and Ad Valorem. A third part prints essays on the maintenance of life, wealth, money, and riches, afterwards revised as Munera Pulveris. Ruskin's case against the science of getting rich runs through all of them.
37106-little-women-or-meg-jo-beth-and-am:
Louisa Alcott wrote Little Women, the story of the four March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy. The hosted copy is the Little, Brown edition with copyright 1880 and more than two hundred pictures by Frank Merrill, plus a view of the March home by Edmund Garrett. A short preface verse, borrowed from John Bunyan, sends the book out like a small pilgrim.

The forty seven chapters run in two parts, from Playing Pilgrims and a merry Christmas through school, work, first love, and loss. The girls grow up one trial at a time while their father serves in the war. Few American novels have stayed in print and in young hands so steadily.
38109-lecture-on-artificial-flight-given:
A lecture pamphlet by Wm G Krueger, delivered at San Francisco in 1876. The Academy of Natural Sciences heard it on August seventh. Krueger spoke by request, with a model of his own invention. Twenty-one sections divide the address. Fable and history open the survey. The balloon's discovery and noted air voyages follow.

Parachutes and kites earn short sections each. Balloons are then declared impracticable for true flight. Fundamental principles come next: weight, surface, and power. Flying creatures' proportions and movements supply the evidence. Present flying machines get a defects list. The practical air ship of the near future closes the prophecy. Krueger begs pardon for a first lecture's faults. Inventors wrestling with flight deserved public money, he argues.
39188-guide-to-west-point-and-the-u-s-mi:
Guide to West Point and the United States Military Academy, with maps and engravings, was published by Van Nostrand in New York in 1867. West Point stands fifty one miles above New York, on the west bank of the Hudson, on a bold shelving plateau.

West Point, the property of the United States by purchase, holds a double interest. It was a key post in the American Revolution, and it is the seat of the National Military Academy. Ninety years before, commissioners from the Provincial Congress of New York first gave the wild spot a public interest. The Hudson was then the main channel between the theatre of war and the country to the north. As a strategic line it parted New England from the more productive south west. Both sides therefore sought to control it, and the gorge called Wey Gat, or Wind Gate, mattered early.
39801-fighting-with-french-a-tale-of-the:
Fighting with French, subtitled A Tale of the New Army, is a war novel by Herbert Strang. Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton put it out in London. Colour pictures by Cyrus Cuneo light the tale through its length. The book first came out in 1915, in the war's second year. Twenty-two chapters run from a chance meeting to a marked-down end.

Stoneway enlists early, and the tale takes him to the back of the front. Bagging a sniper, a fight for a village, and an attic in France follow. A medal chapter, a lost Ginger, and hot work crowd the mid list. Kenneth Amory learns jujutsu from Mr Kishimaru in the first scene. War craft from the East meets the new army's raw young men. Dogged work and transport lorry tricks fill the later chapters.
4075-the-intrusion-of-jimmy:
A comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse, The Intrusion of Jimmy, opens in farce, as a cyclone of a man bursts into a room and shifts a footstool, a small chair, a rug, and Spike. A massive boot sends the chair whirling to the wall, the rug crumples, and Spike lands on all fours, blinking.

Jimmy, gentleman burglar turned good fellow, blunders into love, society, and crime in New York. Wodehouse keeps the pace fast and the talk bright, with crooks and debutantes trading quips. Readers who enjoy light, funny adventure will find an early Wodehouse romp, full of charm and harmless mischief.
40954-potential-enemy:
Mack Reynolds prefaces his story with a sidenote on the conqueror's trap, headed by Caesar's unsolved problem. Alexander, it argues, could not stop after Asia Minor: powerful neighbors might threaten him tomorrow. So he took Egypt and the eastern satrapies, then India, and died at Babylon planning Arabia, Carthage, and Rome.

Orbit printed the tale in its first volume in 1953, and Rome, Napoleon, and Adolf the Aryan join the sidenote's roll. The story proper follows Markham Gray, a freelance journalist riding home from Triton to Earth. Travel itself, the narrator insists, is boring in any century, by spaceship as by train. Gray arms himself with cards, books, chess problems, and wire tapes against the sameness.
41936-principles-of-political-economy:
Principles of Political Economy, by Arthur Latham Perry of Williams College, was copyrighted in 1890 and published in New York in 1891. Front ads list Perry's works, from an introduction at a dollar fifty to a large political economy in its twenty-first edition. A Whittier motto praises work where hand and brain share honor and simple manhood outweighs gold.

Perry dedicates the book to his friend Sterling Morton of Nebraska, founder of Arbor Day. His preface notes that twenty-five years have passed since his first book on these topics, Elements of Political Economy, drawn like a bow at a venture. He had taught history and political economy for a dozen years before that. The text is a full college course in wealth, labor, and trade.
42368-narrative-of-the-suffering-defeat-:
William Atherton wrote a narrative of the suffering and defeat of the North-Western Army under General Winchester. The book was printed for the author at Frankfort, Kentucky, in 1842. Atherton had lived through the campaign and through sixteen months held prisoner by the Indians and the British.

Atherton says history had told the army's suffering only in broad terms, so he gives the detail of his own detachment. He traces the march from Kentucky and the defeat that followed. He tells what he saw at the massacre at the Raisin, naming brave men whose deaths he witnessed with his own eyes. He also charges British officers with conduct worse than that of their Indian allies. Readers get a stark firsthand record of the War of 1812 in the west, written so a new generation would know what their fathers endured.
4362-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-ge:
Philip Henry Sheridan wrote these personal memoirs of his part in the great events of three decades, above all the American Civil War. In his preface he admits the difficulty of recounting his own share without giving his acts too much weight or writing a full history of the years. He leaves readers to judge how well he met that difficulty.

Sheridan offers a record penned by his own hand, of a fight to keep the nation whole, defend liberty, and secure equal political rights. He claims no literary merit, only the importance of the events themselves. The memoirs give a general's view of campaigns, commands, and comrades, and they remain a central source for the Union war.
44991-lily-norris-enemy:
Lily Norris' Enemy, by Joanna Mathews, is a children's tale in the Little Sunbeams set, issued in New York in 1883. Mathews also wrote the Bessie Books and the Flowerets tales on the commandments. The book's motto is: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might. A front plate shows Lily Norris herself.

Front ads for Mathews' other sets praise her child world as real and warm, with children who talk and act in a natural way. Her tales show good acts growing in steady, complete form that young readers might copy. In that spirit, Lily's tale turns on a foe to be faced with work, faith, and a willing heart, in the firm moral style of its day.
45071-the-lost-army:
The Lost Army, a boys' war novel by Thomas Knox, was published in New York in 1899 with pictures. The tale opens in Dubuque, Iowa, on a fine morning in early 1861, as two boys talk of enlisting. Jack Wilson and Harry Fulton, not yet sixteen, have been friends for ten years and work side by side in the same shop.

The Civil War has just begun, after Lincoln's election drove southern states to secede, South Carolina first on December 20. The boys hope the army will take them, or at least find them useful about camp. Knox, a famed war reporter, builds a youth's-eye tale of enlistment, camps, and loss on firm fact.
45356-new-theories-in-astronomy:
William Stirling wrote New Theories in Astronomy, a late life brief against set star lore. E and F N Spon issued the book in London and New York in nineteen hundred six. Stirling was a civil engineer who built rail roads in South America. He died at Lima, Peru, on October seventh, nineteen hundred.

Friends printed his draft as a stone to his name and thought. Chapter one weighs how the earth’s weight was found by plumb lines. Airy’s Harton mine tests, he claims, rest on a plain flaw. Text books pass the flaw on with no fresh check, he charges. A mote in a hollow globe still feels pull, he argues next. The moon can have no spin on its axis, chapter two holds. Set belief says it has, and he sets out to prove it wrong.
46423-a-contribution-to-the-critique-of-:
Charles Kerr and Company of Chicago issued Karl Marx's Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy in 1904. Stone translated it from the second German edition. Kautsky had published that edition in 1897, with changes Marx marked in his own copy.

An appendix adds Marx's introduction to the critique, printed from his posthumous papers. The translator's preface notes the work first appeared in 1859 as the first instalment of a larger project. That project became Capital. The famous preface here states the materialist view of history in a few pages: the base of production shaping law, politics, and thought. Few short texts have been argued over longer. The 1859 preface alone keeps the book in print.
47266-four-introductory-lectures-on-poli:
Nassau Senior, late fellow of Magdalen College and Oxford's chair of political economy, gave these four talks at his university. Longman printed them in London in 1852. They form a first guide to the study of wealth: what it is, how it grows, and how it is shared.

The first talk asks why the field grew so slowly. Its facts are as old as men, Senior says, and laws and customs have flowed from loose views of them for ages. Not till the mid 1700s did any man try to set those views in a frame. Senior gives Quesnay the honour of the first try at a full account of wealth's laws.
48467-boys-of-oakdale-academy:
Morgan Scott wrote a boys' tale of school life at Oakdale Academy. The book came out in New York in 1911. Martin Lewis made four plates for it. Scott had wrote Ben Stone at Oakdale in the same world. A front plate shows a boy in a long, grand leap through the air.

A boy of mystery starts the tale, and Rod's great jump comes soon. The boy who said no, a trap in wait, and a jest gone wrong build strife. A white mark of fear and a doubt arc fill the mid parts. Snow, a close call, and a Grant in fight close the run. School boys get sport, grit, and fun.
49045-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
The Book of Deuteronomy, in the Expositor's Bible series, is a commentary by Andrew Harper. Harper was professor of Hebrew and Old Testament study at Ormond College in the University of Melbourne. Nicoll edited the series, and Armstrong published this volume at New York in 1895. Harper dedicates it to his old teacher Davidson of Edinburgh, in grateful memory of his instruction.

In his preface Harper says a fit exposition of Deuteronomy must treat many topics at once. The limits of the volume forced choice and compression. He dropped a whole chapter on miracle in the Old Testament, since it bore no special tie to this book. Yet he kept both the critical and the digging questions, and the bearing of the book's laws on the faith of the race. He also kept its lessons for the dangers and duties of his own age.
49348-regimental-nicknames-and-tradition:
Regimental Nicknames and Traditions of the British Army is a handbook of the pet names, customs, and honours of every regiment in the service. This fifth edition, enlarged and revised, was published by Gale and Polden at London and Aldershot in 1916. It sold for two shillings.

A photograph of the King as field-marshal fronts the book. The contents run in alphabetical order from the Alexandra, Princess of Wales's Own Yorkshire Regiment to the yeomanry. Cavalry come first in the body of the work: the King's Dragoon Guards, the Queen's Bays, the Carabiniers, the Royal Scots Greys, and the Inniskillings. Guards, line infantry, Highlanders, and the corps follow: medical, ordnance, pay, service, and veterinary. Each entry gives the regiment's nicknames and the stories and traditions behind them.
51056-the-battles-of-the-british-army:
The Battles of the British Army, by Robert Melvin Blackwood, author of The British Army at Home and Abroad and Some Great Commanders. It is a popular account of all the principal engagements of the last hundred years. The third edition was published by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company in London.

The preface weighs war's place in the building of the empire. The arts of peace, justice, and respect for right have done much, Blackwood grants. But the ordinance of battle has had no small share too. Many conflicts, he argues, were thrust upon Britain rather than sought. Wise men call the appeal to arms a deplorable necessity, a last resort when peaceful settlement fails. The volume gives separate, popularly written narratives of the principal engagements. British soldiers, he holds, have never been surpassed for bravery and pluck.
51087-history-of-the-scottish-regiments-:
Murray wrote a past of the Scots corps in the British army's ranks. His book came out in Glasgow in 1862. Murray held a major's rank in the Lanarkshire guards by will. His mate officers begged the book's print, the title page says. A plate fronts the work in full war dress of the age.

The Scots Greys, horse guards of the north, lead his list. The Guards come next: Grenadiers, Coldstreams, and Scots Fusiliers. The First, or Royal Scots, take their long due in turn. Each corps gets its birth, flags, fights, and famed men. March routes and great fields crowd the corps tales in full. Scots war fans get a proud store.
51140-the-bible-and-polygamy-does-the-bi:
The Bible and Polygamy prints a public discussion on the question: does the Bible sanction polygamy? Professor Orson Pratt, one of the Twelve Apostles of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, debated the Reverend Doctor J P Newman, chaplain of the United States Senate. They met in the New Tabernacle at Salt Lake City on August 12, 13, and 14, 1870.

The pamphlet opens with the correspondence that made the debate. Newman wrote to Brigham Young accepting what he took for a challenge in the Salt Lake Daily Telegraph. Young answered that no challenge was his: the paper was not his journal. The discussion proceeded against Pratt instead. Three sermons on the same subject are added, by President George A Smith and Elders Orson Pratt and George Q Cannon, and the book appeared at Salt Lake City in 1874.
51165-the-regimental-records-of-the-brit:
John Farmer compiled these regimental records of the British Army, a historical resume arranged in time order of titles, campaigns, honours, uniforms, facings, badges, and nicknames. Grant Richards published the book at London in 1901. The contents divide the army into cavalry, royal artillery, royal engineers, foot guards, and territorial regiments, with appendices of former numbers and the order of precedence.

The cavalry section opens with the First Life Guards, tracing its titles from His Majesty's Own Troop of Guards in 1660 to the First Life Guards from 1788. Its principal campaigns list Maestricht in 1673, the Boyne in 1690, Flanders and Steenkirk, Neer Landen, and the starred honours Dettingen in 1743 and the Peninsula. Every regiment in the book gets the same compact treatment, so a reader can compare titles, battle honours, and distinctions across the whole army at a glance.
51769-the-auxilia-of-the-roman-imperial-:
Cheesman, fellow and lecturer of New College, Oxford, wrote this study of the auxiliary forces of the Roman army for the Clarendon Press in 1914. A tombstone of a trooper of the Ala Noricorum at Mainz fronts the book. The auxilia were the non-citizen regiments of the empire, horse and foot, and Cheesman begins with the reforms of Augustus that created them.

Four sections treat the auxilia across the first two centuries. Strength and organization of the regiments come first, then recruiting and distribution. Their use for war and frontier defence follows, and arms and armour close the survey. A conclusion takes up the break-up of the Augustan system. Cheesman argues that the subject is more than drill-book detail: it asks how far a ruling race can safely arm its subjects, and what the bargain does to both. The diplomata and the inscriptions are his evidence.
52696-joffre-and-his-army:
Joffre and His Army is a war book by Charles Dawbarn, author of France at Bay, issued at London in 1916. It is dedicated, by permission, to the memory of General Gallieni. The foreword states the book's errand in simple terms. It is meant as a presentation card to the French army, Dawbarn writes. It is a plain story for plain people, with a set shunning of hard terms.

In it the reader will find the leading figures in the fighting order of France, he says. Joffre and his most brilliant helpers stand first. He has tried to render just honour to the poilu, the French common soldier, as well. That man, whose deeds will inspire poets for many a long year, is no soldier by trade. He is drawn from the most peaceful callings, Dawbarn notes with feeling.
52723-the-story-of-the-british-army:
Lieutenant-Colonel Cooper King wrote this story of the British Army, published by Methuen at London in 1897 with plans and illustrations. He dedicated it to Field Marshal Viscount Wolseley, the army's commander-in-chief, whose portrait fronts the volume. Twenty chapters carry the army from the fyrd to the present day.

King begins with the army of the people to the year 1100, passes to the army of the nobles and the Puritan host, then to Marlborough and his men. The Peninsular army gets three chapters, its making, training, and reward, and the army in the Netherlands closes with Waterloo in 1815. The long peace, the Crimea, and three chapters on India under the East India Company and after follow. Appendices list the principal campaigns since 1658, the regiments with their present and former titles, and the badges, mottoes, and nicknames of the army.
5434-the-physiology-of-taste-or-transcen:
Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin wrote The Physiology of Taste, translated from the last Paris edition by Fayette Robinson, as a witty science of eating. The book opens with aphorisms from the professor, a dialogue with his friend, and a biography, then moves into meditations on the senses, taste, and the pleasures of the table. Anecdotes about artists and statesmen illustrate the argument.

Later sections cover pot-au-feu, fowls, game, fish, truffles, sugar, coffee, and chocolate, with recipes and reflections alongside. Brillat-Savarin treats gastronomy as a serious subject and a joyful one. Readers get a classic of food writing, learned, funny, and still quoted at dinner tables.
54721-the-food-question-health-and-econo:
Pacific Press issued The Food Question: Health and Economy in 1917, with work by eight specialists. Doctor Ray Lyman Wilbur of Stanford, then an aide to Herbert Hoover in food work, praised the proofs in a letter used as the frontispiece. The book was planned before food saving became a mass concern.

Chapters cover food economy, food elements, and simple diet, with tables for grains, beans, fruits, nuts, and greens. Later parts treat vitamines and calories, fruit in the diet, and ten reasons for a fleshless diet. H S Anderson gives plain menus and recipes. Closing pages show how to use left-overs and end with a call from Doctor Anna Howard Shaw.
58393-the-mirror-of-alchimy:
The Mirror of Alchimy is a short alchemical treatise printed at London in 1597 for Richard Olive. Its title page ascribes it to Roger Bacon, the famous friar of Merton College and Brasenose College, Oxford. A learned discourse on the force and efficacy of art and nature, by the same hand, is printed with it. Other treatises of the like argument follow. The preface warns that the old philosophers spoke in riddles and cloudy voices on purpose.

The Mirror itself runs to seven chapters on the transmutation of metals. Its first chapter gathers the definitions of the art given in ancient books, beginning with Hermes. The reader is told to fix his mind on the beginning, middle, and end until the subtlety satisfies. The little volume shows how Elizabethan England read medieval alchemy: as hidden wisdom, worth the labor of decoding.
58632-the-maryland-line-in-the-confedera:
Goldsborough, a major in the late Confederate army, wrote The Maryland Line in the Confederate States Army, printed at Baltimore in 1869. He gave the pages to Major-General Isaac Trimble, the soldier without fear and without reproach. Contents treat the First and Second Maryland Infantry, the cavalry battalion, and the Baltimore Light Artillery.

Almost four years after Lee's surrender at Appomattox, nothing yet shows the prominent part Maryland's sons took in the Great Rebellion, the introduction complains. Casualty lists of officers, changes in the battalion, and its state at the war's close fill the record sections. Atkins' brigade at Second Manassas earns a chapter of its own here. Civil War readers get a Maryland Confederate memorial.
58810-the-heavens-above-a-popular-handbo:
The Heavens Above, by Gillet and Rolfe, was published in 1882. Potter and Ainsworth issued the handbook at New York and Chicago. Gillet taught physics at the Normal College in New York. Rolfe had headed a high school at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Six lithographic plates and 460 wood engravings fill the book. The preface states the aim plainly. A brief, simple, and true account of the heavens is promised. Nothing lies beyond a reader of ordinary sense, the authors hold. Dry mathematics are carefully avoided. Yet the methods of astronomers are made clear. Telescopes and spectroscopes are described, and their use explained.

The plates are reductions of work from the Cambridge observatory. One shows the spectra of various lights. The handbook served the general reader of its day.
58944-the-living-mummy:
Ambrose Pratt's novel, in a second edition from Stokes in New York, copyrighted in 1910, with four colour pictures by Louis Fancher, opens in the Libyan desert. The narrator is finishing the translation of a stele of Amen-hotep the Third, which he dug up himself, when his servant Migdal Abu announces visitors. A card is handed in: Sir Robert Ottley has ridden up on an ass, with a woman, after nine weeks without a European sighting.

Ottley is the great Egyptologist and explorer, a decipherer of cuneiform and a millionaire whose spending on learning had doubled its store in ten years. The contents promise the son of Hap, a sarcophagus's perfume, the capture of the coffin, a séance, and the mummy talking. Later chapters give a pleasant chat with a murderer and a rescue by fire.
59212-a-short-history-of-astronomy:
Arthur Berry, a fellow of King's College, Cambridge, wrote a short history of astronomy issued in New York in 1899. He aims at readers with no special grasp of the stars or of maths, who can still follow plain reasoning. His preface owns that a small book must leave much out.

Berry gives only a brief look at the star lore of Egypt, China, and the East, since scholars still dispute what the old records mean. From there he traces the science through its main steps to his own day. The book suits a reader who wants the shape of the field without its sums. Its clear plan made it a standard short guide.
59575-dearest-enemy:
Fox B Holden traps a space trainee above a burning Earth in a tale from Worlds of If Science Fiction, October 1956. The headnote twists an old stage rule: the show must go on, but what is the point when your audience is very, very dead?

A buzzer throbs in the metal shell of Vanguard-I. It repeats like a trapped wasp, though no wasps live in orbit. The man at the refractor keeps watching, sweating, unable to stop. Red gouts of flame stipple the Atlantic seaboard below, button by button. They branch and riddle westward. Others drift east from the Pacific, as if groping toward a planned meeting. If he silences the buzzer and answers, another man's voice will make it real. It will no longer be a final training film. He and Streeter were chosen, and the eliminations were over.
60166-the-ordeal-by-fire-by-a-sergeant-i:
Marcel Berger, a sergeant in the French Army, wrote The Ordeal by Fire, rendered into English by Mrs Cecil Curtis. G P Putnams Sons in New York and London issued the book in nineteen seventeen, with a copyright of nineteen sixteen. The tale runs day by day from August first, nineteen fourteen. Parts and books divide the march to war. Chapter names mark each stage of the road.

Early chapters show Jeannine Landry, a young man of nineteen fourteen, and bells in a mountain village. Berger then rides back by train, sees Paris, his father, and his friend. Later books take him to billets, alarms, and the firing line. A baptism of fire, a victorious dawn, and a night on outpost duty close the head contents. Readers get a foot soldier view of the first weeks of the Great War.
60320-a-plea-for-monogamy:
Wilfrid Lay wrote A Plea for Monogamy, for Boni and Liveright at New York in 1923. Lay had written on the unconscious mind and spirit before it. The first printing came in June 1923, and printings ran on into 1926. A Browning verse heads the book: love is best, it cries. The dedication is Latin, to his most beloved wife.

Chapter one treats the true conception of marriage in numbered sections. Disproportion of feeling and schooling, archaic emotions, and charity stand there. The sexual crisis and a man's erotic dominance take their sections. Marriage the only cure, and the normal sex life, follow in the list. Chapter two turns to modern emotional unrest and discontented wives. Playmates, honeymoons, and barter in love take their heads as well. Lay pleads one marriage, kept whole, against the fashions of his day.
60949-notes-on-veterinary-anatomy:
Charles Korinek, a graduate of the Ontario Veterinary College, wrote these notes on veterinary anatomy. The Veterinary Science Association of America issued them, copyrighted in 1917. Korinek had sixteen years of practice as a veterinary surgeon and had served as state veterinarian for Oregon.

Eight chapters cover the horse's frame in order: bones, joints, muscles, inner organs, blood vessels, nerves, and senses. A last chapter treats the growth of the foal before birth. Seven plates show the skeleton, the muscles, the heart, and the foot. The book served students and working vets who needed a short, clear guide.
61836-chicago-and-its-cess-pools-of-infa:
Samuel Paynter Wilson wrote Chicago and Its Cess-Pools of Infamy, a blast at vice in his town. Wilson issued the sixteenth edition in Chicago himself. He had written Chicago by Gas Light before this book. A club chief’s letter at the front praises his work.

Wilson says no book can tell the whole truth of the town. Chapters map high life and low dives side by side. The white slave trade takes the longest, hardest part. He tells how that trade was smashed in raids. Why girls go astray fills one grim chapter. Gambling dens, pawn shops, and dance halls follow. A rescue mission gives one bright note. Churches and divorce courts close his tour of shame.
63456-andreas-vesalius-the-reformer-of-a:
James Moores Ball published 'Andreas Vesalius, the Reformer of Anatomy' with the Medical Science Press at Saint Louis in 1910, dedicated to the fathers of anatomy and the artist-anatomists. An introduction treats the study of medical history and the anatomical renaissance within the general one. A survey of ancient anatomy follows, from Egypt and Greece through Hippocrates, Alcmaeon, and Aristotle to Herophilus, Erasistratus, and Galen.

Mondino, the restorer of anatomy, and his successors Zerbi, Achillinus, Berengario da Carpi, and Estienne carry the story to Vesalius himself. Ball follows the young anatomist from Louvain to Paris, where Sylvius and Fernel taught, then to the professor's chair at Padua. The anatomical plates of 1538, extensively pirated, precede the great chapter: the manuscript and illustrations of the Fabrica carried to Basel and printed by Oporinus, their beauty long ascribed wrongly to Titian.
63615-a-century-s-progress-in-astronomy:
A Century's Progress in Astronomy is a small history by Macpherson, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1906. Blackwood issued it. Macpherson also wrote Astronomers of To-Day. His preface, dated Balerno in October 1906, states the book's aim in one line.

He wished to present, in small compass, a record of the great progress in astronomy during the past hundred years. He thanks the works of Newcomb, Schiaparelli, Lowell, Young, Ball, Gore, Flammarion, and Clerke. The first chapters treat Herschel, the pioneer and discoverer. Herschel found Uranus, gauged the stars, and mapped clusters and nebulae. The sun's spots and spectrum take later chapters. Macpherson tells a century of discovery plainly.
64577-the-new-astronomy:
The New Astronomy, by Samuel Pierpont Langley, director of the Allegheny Observatory, was published at Boston in 1888. Its chapters had appeared in the Century magazine over the previous four years. The contents treat the sun's surroundings, the sun's energy in two chapters, the planets and the moon, and the stars. An index and a list of illustrations close the book.

Langley writes for the educated public, not the professional reader. His preface complains that support flows to the old astronomy, already richly endowed. The new astronomy, so fruitful in results, struggles almost unaided, like a younger sister without a portion. By the new he means the physical study of the sun and stars, their heat, light, and makeup, rather than mere positions. The book argues the case for that younger science while teaching its findings, above all about the sun's energy.
64649-the-herschels-and-modern-astronomy:
Agnes Clerke wrote a life of the Herschels for the Century Science Series, issued at London in 1895. Henry Roscoe edited the series, whose other volumes treat Dalton, Faraday, Lyell, and Darwin. A portrait of Sir William Herschel at fifty, after Abbott's painting, fronts the book.

Clerke names her chief authority in the preface: the memoir of Caroline Herschel published in 1876, which carries Caroline's journals and recollections. William himself, she notes, referred to his sister for dates of his early life. Other sources are few and meagre, yielding gleanings worth collecting. Brother and sister together remade astronomy, and Clerke tells their work as one story.
65250-recipes-used-in-the-cooking-school:
Recipes Used in the Cooking Schools, United States Army, is an official cookbook issued at Washington in 1906. The Government Printing Office printed the book for the army schools. Its contents list is a full map of army cooking in that era. Soups, fish and oysters, sauces, and gravies open the order of the book.

Recipes named for soups are bean, beef, bouillon, pea, potato, rice, Spanish, and two kinds of tomato. Fish dishes take in codfish balls, boiled and creamed salmon, salmon croquettes, and oyster potpie. Sauces include an army sauce, an army chocolate sauce, cream, egg, Spanish, and white sauces. The sample bean soup recipe soaks three pounds of beans overnight in two quarts of water. It then boils them for about two hours in fresh water, a plain style fitted to cooking for hundreds of men at once.
65980-the-invisible-enemy:
Arnold Castle wrote this science fiction tale, The Invisible Enemy, printed in the October 1954 number of Imagination. A blurb at the head sets its puzzle. At fifteen a boy was sent to war to fight an enemy he could not understand. Stranger still was the victory to be won after he met defeat.

It was the day, the tale begins. A car carries Tom and his parents slowly down a quiet morning street. His father recalls his own war and wonders how like it Tom's will be. His mother pictures her son in a foxhole under the next great weapon. Tom hides his nerves and refuses to let them come in with him. He walks up the steps of a building marked Department of Peace. Words over its door wish the age of violence to stay history.
66824-comet-lore-halley-s-comet-in-histo:
Comet Lore, Halley's comet in history and astronomy, is a popular science book by Edwin Emerson, issued at New York in 1910. A picture shows the comet of that year as seen in New York, looking west in late May. Emerson had written a history of the nineteenth century. His contents open with Halley's comet itself, then turn to the terror of the comet.

Famous comets of olden times follow in the list. The book thus joins two strands: the hard astronomy of a comet whose return men could foretell, and the long fear of comets as signs of doom. The year 1910 saw the comet's return and a wave of public dread, with the earth due to pass through its tail. Emerson wrote for the crowd that looked west in May and wondered.
67404-cavalry-curt-or-the-wizard-scout-o:
Cavalry Curt, or The Wizard Scout of the Army is a dime novel by Waldo Browne, issued in the Gem Library by Sibley and Son of New York. The number is dated January 9, 1892, and priced at five cents. The cover bills it as a great war story of Sherman's march to the sea. Browne also wrote The Swordsman of Toledo and Border Knights.

The first chapter, Running the Gantlet, sets the scene like a playbill. The time is daybreak on May 6, 1864. The place is a wild, broken country in northern Georgia. Advance, friend, and give the countersign, he calls. The sentry's shot flies wide and the man is hurled to earth. One of Sherman's scouts, their leader shouts. The tale runs at that gallop.
68164-in-the-volcano-s-mouth-or-a-boy-ag:
Frank Sheridan wrote this boys' story, number 134 in Street and Smith's Bound-to-Win Library, a weekly series of copyrighted adventure stories for boys. Its full title adds a subtitle: or, a boy against an army.

The publisher's pages pitch the line directly: bright, clean stories showing what a pure-minded lad with courage and mettle can do. Neighboring numbers in the list include Muscles of Steel, The Boys' Revolt, and With the Mad Mullah, by hands like Harrie Irving Hancock and Weldon Cobb. Sheridan also wrote Tom Scott, the American Robinson Crusoe, for the series. The volcano's mouth promises the setting; the army promises the odds. Boys of the dime-novel era get their weekly adventure, bound to win.
7076-prisoner-for-blasphemy:
George William Foote tells his story as a prisoner for blasphemy, first published in 1886 by the Progressive Publishing Company of London. A Byron line at the head holds that persecution is not refutation, nor even triumph, and that the wretched infidel may be happier in prison than the proudest assailant. The chapters run from the storm brewing and a first summons through indictment, trial at the Old Bailey, and Newgate.

Later chapters follow a second trial, the Black Maria, Holloway Gaol, prison life, Parson Plaford, and a third trial, closing with loss and gain, a long night, and daylight. Foote calls the tale strange, since only three living Englishmen knew a blasphemy prisoner's lot, and painful, since unmerited suffering shames a boasted age of freedom.
71154-lectures-on-painting-delivered-at-:
Henry Fuseli gave talks on paint craft at the Royal Academy in London. A plate shows him cut by Sievier from a small work of Haughton. That plate came out on May 1, 1820, in the Strand. More notes and watch words fill this form of his talks. A first part scans what craft lore old and new hands hold.

A short sketch, not a whole plan, is all he claims to give. Men of taste need less of it than young hands at the craft. Tools, forms, and the great old chiefs fill his keen talks. Each talk was made to be heard by men at their boards. His fierce taste ruled the taste of his whole school age. Art youth got a strong guide.
71442-an-english-woman-sergeant-in-the-s:
An English Woman-Sergeant in the Serbian Army, by Flora Sandes, tells her war service in her own words. An intro by Slavko Grouitch, of the Serbian foreign ministry, opens the book. Chapter one rejoins the Serbians in November 1915. Sandes had worked in Serbian hospitals since the start of the war. She hurried back from leave as Bulgaria entered the fight. Her ship carried shells as well as passengers, and submarines hunted it.

Chapters follow the second regimental ambulance into retreat. A ride to Kalabac and a battle in snow come next. The army then crosses the Albanian mountains toward the coast. Christmas at Durazzo, plane raids, and the move to Corfu close the account. Sandes writes of cold, hunger, and duty shared with Serbian troops.
71599-kitty-s-enemy:
Kitty's Enemy: or, The Boy Next Door, by Eleanora H Stooke, was first published by S W Partridge at London in September 1911 and frequently reprinted. The frontispiece shows Mr Dottin shaking his fist at his late visitors and shutting the door on them.

Kitty Glanville, ten years old, blue-eyed and fair, gardens with her brother Bob in plots behind their semi-detached villa during the Easter holidays. The chapters move through that dreadful boy, Tim's revenge, and Kitty interviewing Tim. A spoilt plan, a covered basket, and Kitty's accident follow. Snip intrudes, Kitty asks Tim's forgiveness, and Tim entertains, before the conclusion calls him a regular brick.
72902-learning-to-fly-in-the-u-s-army:
Learning to Fly in the United States Army is a manual of flying practice by Fales. The author had taught machine engineering and the chair of air studies at the University of Illinois. McGraw-Hill published the first edition at New York in 1917. A frontispiece shows a group of army student flyers.

The contents begin with a short history of flight, from early trials to the last twenty years of real progress. Chapters then treat types of war planes and the rules of flight. Middle parts cover flying the machine and cross country work. Later chapters turn to rigging, materials, and raising a plane from parts. Closing parts treat truing the body, handling planes in the field, and inspection. The book served the rush of new army flyers in the war years.
75996-a-text-book-of-veterinary-anatomy:
A Text-Book of Veterinary Anatomy, by Septimus Sisson, professor of comparative anatomy at Ohio State University, was published by Saunders in 1911. Sisson covers the horse in depth and then the ox, sheep, pig, and dog, with 588 illustrations, many in color. The book served students and practicing veterinarians as a complete reference.

Its sections run from joints and ligaments through muscles to the digestive, respiratory, and other systems, organ by organ and species by species. The level of detail, down to individual glands and vessels, made it a laboratory companion as much as a reading text. Sisson's anatomy became the standard work in its field for decades, and later editions carried his name long after this first one.
76843-the-army-behind-the-army:
The Army Behind the Army is a book on the support services of the American army by Major Powell, published by Scribner's in New York in 1919. Powell also wrote Fighting in Flanders and Italy at War. The book is dedicated to five friends of the American Expeditionary Force, in memory of days on the banks of the Marne.

Each chapter was written with the help of the chief of the branch it treats, the author notes. Those chiefs read and revised the chapters, so the figures stand as nearly exact as could be made. The book explains the supply, transport, and labour troops behind the fighting line. A picture shows the burning of an observation balloon at Fort Sill.
77516-astronomy:
Astronomy is a volume of the Concise Knowledge Library, printed at New York in 1898. Clerke, Fowler, and Gore wrote it. Clerke had already written a popular history of astronomy in the nineteenth century. Fowler taught at the Royal College of Science, and Gore wrote The Scenery of the Heavens. A moon photograph from Paris fronts the book.

Clerke opens with a short history of the science from Hipparchus to her own time. Fowler then outlines spherical and gravitational astronomy, with the instruments observers use. Clerke returns for the solar system, and Gore closes with the sidereal heavens. Diagrams and photographs fill the pages, made expressly for this volume.
77743-duval-s-artistic-anatomy:
Mathias Duval's artistic anatomy was revised and enlarged by A Melville Paterson, late professor of anatomy at Liverpool. The book first appeared in September 1884 and was reprinted many times. A revised edition came in 1905, with later printings through 1919. Duval's preface says the work sums up ten years of lectures at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris.

Duval thanks his listeners for the exchange of ideas that taught him their needs. The book is for artists who have already drawn the human form from the antique and from life. It explains forms, attitudes, and movements rather than describing each region. Duval calls his method synthesis, not analysis.
77802-no-enemy:
Ford Madox Ford wrote No Enemy, a tale of reconstruction, issued in New York in 1929. Ford also wrote No More Parades and Some Do Not. He gives the book to Esther Julia Madox Ford, in a letter dated June 21, 1929. Ford says the pages show what the world seemed like as she was preparing to enter it.

Part one, Four Landscapes, introduces Gringoire, a poet and Gallophile who went to the war. Gringoire now lives in rural quiet in a house like the gingerbread cottage of Haensel and Gretel. Ford says men hear of soldiers at war, but seldom of how it left them. His compiler visits on Saturday afternoons to record the painful work of rebuilding.
78032-twelve-years-in-the-army:
Twelve Years in the Army, or the incidents of a soldier life, is a memoir by John Gollan. Gollan was late corporal in the 79th Cameron Highlanders, as the title page states. The book was printed at Elgin in Scotland in 1864 at the Morayshire Advertiser office. A verse motto on leaving home in youth and finding all changed stands at its front.

In his preface Gollan throws himself on the indulgence of his readers for his tale. He says he does not wish to enter into the genealogy of his family in the narrative. Friends had asked him for that history on several occasions, as the catalogue sample shows. The memoir promises the incidents of twelve years of service from the ranks. It is a voice from the other ranks of the Victorian army, a class whose own accounts of soldiering are far rarer than those of officers.
7811-the-war-romance-of-the-salvation-ar:
Evangeline Booth, commander of the Salvation Army in America, tells its war work in The War Romance of the Salvation Army, written with Grace Livingston Hill and issued in 1919. A foreword answers a generous public's call, noting the Army sought only thanks from those it helped, not wide fame.

Service is the watchword, Booth writes, and no reward equals doing the most good to the most people in the most need. Through huts, canteens, and front-line help, the book records doughnuts, coffee, comfort, and prayer for troops, and a humble service that won a nation's gratitude.
79645-the-invisible-enemy:
The Invisible Enemy, a science fiction tale by Jerry Sohl, opens above a dangerous planet. A ship has circled the spot at 25000 feet for an hour. Technicians weigh and measure the world below while probes test where no eye can see. Harley Allison sits in the computer room and takes in the stream of data.

He records the readings on magnetic tapes and readies them for the machine. He resents what the commander is trying to do with the survey. The planet below swallows men with no clear menace to fight against. That hook is stated in the blurb at the head of the tale. Allison and his computer must find the unseen enemy before it takes more of the crew.
8005-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
Moses speaks for the last time in Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Bible, as Israel stands on the edge of the Promised Land. The book retells the law given at Sinai, urges the people to remember their deliverance from Egypt, and sets out blessings for obedience and curses for turning away. Its name means second law, since much of it restates earlier commandments for a new generation.

Deuteronomy closes with Moses viewing the land he will not enter and passing leadership to Joshua. Its speeches shaped Jewish and Christian ideas of covenant, the agreement between God and his people. In the King James Version, the long addresses carry a solemn, farewell weight, and the book remains a foundation text for understanding Israel's faith.
8172-history-of-astronomy:
George Forbes, formerly professor of natural philosophy at Anderson's College, Glasgow, wrote this history of astronomy in two periods. Book one, the geometrical period, covers primitive astronomy and astrology, ancient Chinese and Chaldean astronomy, ancient Greek astronomy, and the reign of epicycles from Ptolemy to Copernicus. Book two, the dynamical period, follows the discovery of the true solar system through Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Galileo and the telescope, and notions of gravitation. A portrait of Newton fronts the volume.

Forbes writes for general readers, explaining how humanity moved from sky myths to mathematical law. His history is clear, well ordered, and rich in anecdote. For students of science, it remains a readable classic, and a good guide to the long road from epicycles to Newton.
8232-the-world-english-bible-web-deutero:
Deuteronomy, in the World English Bible, gives Moses' farewell words in modern English, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward. These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the fortieth year, after striking Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan. The book retells the law, recalls the wilderness journey, and warns the new generation to remember, obey, and choose life as they enter the land.

The modern version keeps Deuteronomy's sermon style, with its repeated calls to remember and to love God wholly. Its place names and journeys, from Horeb by Mount Seir to Kadesh Barnea, ground the speeches in geography. For readers meeting the book fresh, this rendering offers the second law in language that reads like spoken counsel.
8436-speculations-from-political-economy:
C. B. Clarke, a Fellow of the Royal Society, offers nine articles in Speculations from Political Economy, and his introduction warns they are speculations, by no means altogether recommendations. Nearly all were suggested by considering mere propositions of political economy, some old, some given by friends, and Clarke follows each idea where it leads.

The book suits readers who like economics as a thinking game: take a principle, push it, and see what follows. Clarke writes for educated general readers rather than specialists, and his speculations touch policy, trade, and human conduct. It is a Victorian economist's notebook, curious and candid about its own limits.
badge-of-infamy:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction novel, here in its Ace Books paperback form. Feldman, a doctor stripped of his standing, crash-lands on Mars with Chris, bouncing twice and turning over before he frees himself from the seat straps. Oxygen bottles and spacesuits come out of the wreck while the colony's medical authorities close in.

On del Rey's Mars, medicine is a closed guild and unlicensed practice a crime. A magistrate and the official Blane discuss Feldman's case: Dr. Ryan acted quickly, the public is nervous, and showing Feldman responsible while Medical eliminates the infection may stabilise things. The sentence, they agree, will have to be death. A plague, a rebel doctor, and a monopoly that would rather kill than share make a tight, angry parable of professional power.
britannica-1911-autogamy: Autogamy is a botanical term for self-fertilization, the process by which a plant fertilizes itself. The word is built from two Greek parts: autos, meaning self, and gamia, meaning marriage. The entry gives only that definition and the word's construction. It then points the reader onward to the article on angiosperms, the flowering plants, where the processes of fertilization in plants receive their fuller treatment.
britannica-1911-autonomy:
Autonomy in its broad sense means freedom from outside control. It is self-rule. The word joins two Greek parts, for self and for law. Most uses add a word that sets its scope. Political autonomy is self-rule in the widest sense. It leaves no room for rule from outside at all. Local autonomy is a smaller thing. A higher power marks out the field in which it may act. Town councils in England are an example.

A middle kind is seen in the British colonies of the time. Their self-rule stops just short of full freedom from the crown. The word is used in a loose way for churches and like bodies too. Kant gave the word a strict use in thought about right and wrong. For him, the will that is rational is a law to itself. It owes that law to no outside voice.
britannica-1911-belknap-jeremy:
Jeremy Belknap (1744–1798) was an American author and clergyman born at Boston. He graduated from Harvard in 1762 and in 1767 became minister of a Congregational church at Dover, New Hampshire. Twenty years later he moved to the Federal Street church in Boston, where he stayed until his death.

Belknap is remembered as the founder of the Massachusetts Historical Society, and in 1792 he became an overseer of Harvard. His chief books are a History of New Hampshire, printed from 1784 to 1792, and American Biography, covering Americans of note. He also wrote The Foresters, a work of fiction, before dying at Boston in June 1798.
britannica-1911-belleau-remy:
Remy Belleau (about 1527–1577) was a French poet of the Pléiade, born at Nogent-le-Rotrou. He studied with Ronsard under Jean Daurat at the Collège de Coqueret. In 1557 he served with René de Lorraine against Naples, then tutored the young marquis d’Elbœuf, who grew into a patron of poets.

Belleau gave French readers their first Anacreon in 1556 and his Petites inventions a year later, poems on stones, insects and flowers. His best-known work, the Amours et nouveaux échanges des pierres précieuses of 1576, sings of gems, and Ronsard said he built his tomb from those precious stones. Belleau also wrote notes on Ronsard’s Amours of great learning and taste.
britannica-1911-bigamy:
Bigamy, in English law, is the offence of marrying again while a first husband or wife still lives. The word joins the Latin bis, twice, with the Greek gamos, marriage. The governing statute cited is the Offences against the Person Act of 1861. A bigamous second marriage is simply void under church law. An act of 1604 first made the offence a felony. The 1911 Britannica article walks through the law's long history in detail.

In canon law the word once ran wider, catching even a clerk who married a widow. The Council of Lyons in 1274 stripped such bigamists of clergy privilege. An English statute of 1547 restored that privilege in full. The article then covers defences, foreign marriages, and proof in court. An honest belief in a valid divorce works as a defence in some places, but not in others. Continental penalties close the survey.
britannica-1911-blasphemy:
Blasphemy is defined here as evil speaking against God. The entry is chiefly a history of how law has punished it. The word came through French from a Greek term for profane speech. Under Mosaic law the penalty was death by stoning. Justinian's laws kept death as the punishment.

English common law treats blasphemy as a crime. Courts can punish it with fine, prison, and shaming corporal punishment. The entry walks through statutes in order. An act of Edward VI punished reviling the sacrament. An act of 1688 shut deniers of the Trinity out of toleration. The Blasphemy Act of 1697–1698 then penalised professed Christians. It hit those who denied core doctrines in writing or speech. Later pages carry the legal story forward.
britannica-1911-bronchotomy:
Bronchotomy, built from Greek words for the windpipe and for cutting, is a medical term for a surgical incision into the throat. The short entry is chiefly a note on naming: one old, broad word has given way to three sharper ones that say exactly where the cut is made.

Laryngotomy, thyrotomy and tracheotomy have now largely superseded bronchotomy because each indicates the place of incision more accurately. That shift in terms is the whole substance of the notice. Surgical language grew more precise. The operation itself, opening the throat to reach the airway, stayed the same in aim.
britannica-1911-church-army:
Church Army is an organization article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Church Army is an English religious body, founded in 1882. Its founder was the Reverend Wilson Carlile, later a prebendary of St Paul's. He formed working men and women into an orderly army of soldiers and officers.

Their task was to serve as Church of England evangelists. They worked among the outcasts and criminals of the Westminster slums. Carlile held that the lowest classes needed bold new action from the Church. He also believed the work was best done by people of the same class. The Army's rule joined evangelistic zeal with church order. As the work grew, a training school for evangelists opened in Oxford. It soon moved to London, where headquarters stood near Marble Arch. The entry shows a church taking its mission into the streets.
britannica-1911-clot-antoine-barthelemy:
Clot, Antoine Barthélemy (1793–1868) was a French physician, known as Clot Bey, born at Grenoble on 7 November 1793 and graduated in medicine and surgery at Montpellier. After practice at Marseilles he became chief surgeon to Mehemet Ali, viceroy of Egypt. At Abuzabel near Cairo he founded a hospital and schools for all branches of medical instruction, and for French. Despite serious religious difficulties he instituted the study of anatomy by dissection in Egypt.

In 1832 Mehemet Ali gave him the dignity of bey without requiring him to abjure his religion, a marked condition in the award. In 1836 he received the rank of general and was appointed head of the medical administration of the country. He returned to Marseilles in 1849, revisited Egypt in 1856, and died at Marseilles on 28 August 1868. His publications cover cholera epidemics, plague in Egypt, quarantines and ophthalmia across four decades.
britannica-1911-collier-jeremy:
Jeremy Collier (1650–1726) was an English churchman who would not swear to the new king. He was born at Stow-with-Quy in Cambridgeshire on 23 September 1650. He was schooled at the free school at Ipswich, where his father was head, and at Caius College, Cambridge. He took his degrees in 1673 and 1676. After a short time as a private chaplain, he was made rector of Ampton in 1679. In 1685 he became a lecturer at Gray's Inn.

At the Revolution, Collier was sent to Newgate for a tract in favour of James II. That tract was a reply to Bishop Burnet's defence of the place of King William. He was set free after some months in jail, with no trial, by the help of his friends. In the next two years he kept up his attacks on the rule of the day in print.
